### 2026-11-05: # Nov 4: First work and schematic

**4h**

# Nov 4: First work and schematic

Given that week 5 lets us build whatever we want, my brain immediately jumped to more nuclear related projects (I built some for week 1 and 4!), but then I reconsidered and thought - what would be genuinely useful to me?

I decided the answer was an adjustable power supply. It is a very handy thing to have for testing electronics or in general for work (I was recently reverse engineering a network switch and needed a  stable 3.3V source to dump the flash! Fun fact, a Raspberry Pi Pico can work, but it's amperage is very limited). First, I thought of how I would power said supply. I originally wanted USB, but it would get pricy and more complicated fast. So I decided to spare myself the pain and money and I found a Connect IT laptop charger that outputs around 18V on a 5.5/2.5mm barrel jack tip. I decided to use a LM2576T-ADJ buck converter to step it down while still being able to add current limiting that is adjustable. Given that lab supplies and their components are expensive, I decided this project would be fully analog with no microcontroller or firmware. That way, I can save money on the digital side of things and make the supply more powerful.

I started by going through GM Electronic (just like W3/4, it's my local electronics supplier) and picked out every part. The biggest issue like always is the fact that passive components have strict minimum order quantities, especially resistors (1 type of resistor = 10 pcs/2 Kč each, roughly 1$ total for 10). Resistors having a minimum would be bearable, but some components have a minimum much higher and the costs go up fast. I decided I would only use 1k and 10k resistors to save money on other types.

![GM Electronic cart](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/5eb1ba9efb9ec1ad40de329938b928ec88276dad09da6c35366b6c4f3eeceed2.png)

One feature I was planning was undervoltage lockout to make sure that the regulator wouldn't try to run with an input too low. My original idea was using a TL431  as a comparator that would drive the ON and OFF pins of LM2576, but the datasheet of LM2576 sadly clearly says the ON and OFF pin needed to be below 1 volt for the regulator to turn on, and the TL431 can never get its cathode below 2V. To fix this, I removed the LM358P I originally planned for sensing current and replaced it with an LM324N.

With parts picked out and an idea of how the supply would work, I created the KiCad project, made a repo, structured it and started the schematic. For the input stage, I put a simple screw terminal from the DC jack, a RUE300 polyfuse for OCP and I also added reverse polarity protection (w/ IRF9540N).

![Input](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/e514d7d8e6f45aba7d5769ec911a11ca6a29fbe957fe5601b7f0e2c380726b6d.png)

Next I put a LM2576T-ADJ buck converter. I used a TALEMA DPO-3.0-100 inductor and a SB540 Schottky catch diode. I needed a 500 ohm resistance for feedback, so I had to make it in parallel using my two 1k resistors. For undervoltage lockout, I used the C variant of the LM324 op-amp. Below about 7.5V, the comparator output goes HIGH and the regulator is turned off. I added slight hysteresis (a 10k resistor) which gives a turn on about 8.8V and turn off at 6.8 volts.

![Buck section](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/f313d1f569fe78e49c84a1e7889cd4a250c7dd8c95d131388126a370bf687c12.png)

![Under voltage lockout section](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/f459c94d452c5d53732d9383f4475e49b83213b68fa69c2181cbfd59c3c18471.png)

**Next up: Finishing the schematic and assigning footprints.**

**tl;dr: Planned the project, picked all parts, drew the input section, buck converter, undervoltage lockout, added hysteresis**

**Total time spent: ~4 hours**

### 2026-11-05: # Nov 5: Finished schematic and footprints

**5h**

# Nov 5: Finished schematic and footprints

Today I continued where yesterday's work ended, which was still the schematic. First thing to make today was current sensing. I used a 0.1 ohm 3 watt shunt resistor on the output return path and used an op-amp (variant A this time) as a sense amplifier which ended up giving around 1.1V for each ampere. The limit is set by the current potentiometer and sensed current is compared against the setpoint by op-amp variant B. We also use a red LED to show CC mode, but it also blocks current from flowing backwards into the feedback. I originally tried using an SB540 diode but it could possibly leak a bit of current backwards which wouldn't be ideal for my project.

![Current sensing and CC loop part 1](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/fc9c9f3ad38698e382d3f9f7e983d2d8d522979d4e0679632e8b6d6849fa9dd4.png)

![Current sensing and CC loop part 2](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/6fa67d785ca867297fff8e1631abd936dafadb799c8a5e306393afcc86ee56f0.png)

Op-amp variant D is used for buffering the SHOW LIMIT voltage. When the button is pressed, the meter reads the setpoint scaled in a way that 1.00V on our display means 1.00A limit. It's a bit finnicky but it was the best way to avoid paying for another display. However, here came a bigger issue! I originally picked a 1k resistor from VIN to the LED, but after checking the listing of my [LED](https://www.gme.cz/v/1492964/bright-led-bl-b2141-l-led-3mm-zelena), I found out the maximum forward current was only 7 mA, and we would easily exceed that with 18V and a 1k resistor. So I changed it to three 1k resistors in a series which should be enough.

![Fixed green LED](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/af574276d87481bbf9982d4b228568bf6a24b3f3e946a15d214da0ef61c45a46.png)

When wiring the front panel, I used the MTS-102-A2 toggle switch in the output line after the voltage sense point of the meter, which means I can easily set the voltage with the output disconnected and the meter would still show it. For the SHOW LIMIT button, I added a KLS 7-P8.0x8.0 DPDT momentary button. I also added a SB540 diode for reverse protection across the output terminal.

After I was done with the schematic, I ran the electrical rules checker and got two warnings. KiCad unfortunately made the second half of the DPDT button into a separate part (SW3) instead of being the B of SW2, so I had to change the reference manually.

![ERC warnings](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/1f52d43841fffc567042eca27aebb5aaef5a8d909b5f3c49d9db93f05223a1ef.png)

![ERC clean](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/10726718d709175c4c9bd79f2663c2725f669e26026402c09e7e902922242015.png)

Assigning footprints was as always a bit tedious. Most parts were standard KiCad footprints (but of course I still had to assign them), but two parts had no footprints. The MTS-102-A2 toggle and the KLS7 button. I had to make a custom footprint for those, but thankfully I had a good amount of practice with that from week 3 and 4!

![Unassigned footprints](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/eb792da2d8c4725e458372a1adc9b72e55e8ac9453dd2548c53a275ae0232848.png)

![Assigned footprints](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/654984d6c733468a68a5eae912d8296bc691849972f2991d6a897e235aa85250.png)

![Custom footprint for the MTS-102 toggle](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/d365dc9bff1906dcf446fa196f0787cccdc69061735e494275cd82c5c14f9a12.png)

![Custom footprint for the KLS7 button](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/d780f1dbf00c5ae0cb8ccf2fcd717fb629ef0fc84bdf21ee4841b7c9d9a351bf.png)

**Next up: Beginning PCB work.**

**tl;dr: Finished the full schematic with current sensing, CC loop, SHOW LIMIT, LEDs, output, meter), fixed overcurrent on an LED, assigned all footprints, made two custom footprints, cleaned ERC.**

**Total time spent: ~5 hours**
